_comment: Registry for the semantic lifting loop (DECOMP-LIFT-PILOT-001, extended by
One entry per reconstructed translation unit. Function boundaries are never
restated by hand: GBARam's come from config/compiler_probes.json, and the
ByteCodeInterpreter's are re-derived from the ROM on every run and checked
against the recorded extents. See docs/LIFT_LOOP.md.
`compiler` describes the MODERN toolchain configuration only. It is not a
claim about the original compiler, and no result from it may be reported as
`semantic_minimum_checks` is per target on purpose. One global number would
either wave through a truncated run of a small self-check or fail a
`host_build_bits` selects the host toolchain width. A reconstruction that
holds pointers in u32 fields models a 32-bit machine: built 64-bit, the high
half of every stored address is lost and the first dereference through one
faults. This is a property of the machine model, not something to widen away.

targets.name: GBARam allocator
targets.role: small-block heap allocator: initialise, unlink, insert, merge, allocate, free, total free
targets.notes: the first lifted family. Chosen because it is the only region in the ROM map whose boundaries are independently established: eight functions recovered by chain-walk recursive descent, every path terminating, zero gaps, zero undecodable bytes, and one shared 4-word literal pool that proves it was a single translation unit. The surviving original build command names it directly: tcpp -S -c -cpu ARM7TDMI -O1 src/GBARam.c.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter dispatch loop
targets.role: script engine: the bytecode dispatch loop, the dialog entry point that calls it, and one untitled helper sharing the same literal pool
targets.notes: the first real engine subsystem. The ROM preserves the original source path T:\Source\ByteCodeInterpreter\ByteCodeInterpreter.cpp as ASCII at 0x08004160, referenced by the assertion at 0x080040F4. The unit is three functions because they share ONE 8-byte literal pool at 0x08004158, which is what establishes a single compilation unit. The pool is NOT adjacent to the code: two alignment bytes separate them and 86 bytes of unrelated code sit between. The dispatch table at 0x080554C0 has 31 entries, bounded by the UTF-16 assertion string at 0x0805553C. The 31 handler targets and the native table are deliberately NOT decompiled here; the native table is 266 entries, measured and proved by DECOMP-LIFT-SCRIPT-HANDLER-001 (a prior claim of 283 is refuted).

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter primary slot 2
targets.role: the handler that reaches the native dispatch table: consumes a one-byte native index and selects native[index]
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 2, entry 0x08003CBE, 22 bytes and 10 instructions. A separate translation unit from the interpreter: separate code and a separate literal pool at 0x08003F40, which four other primary handlers (slots 21-24) also load from. It is reached ONLY through the primary dispatch table, so a direct-call census correctly returns nothing. Handler 2 never writes r0, so the context is passed to the native routine unchanged; 10 of 12 sampled native routines read r0 before writing it, and none read r2, so r0 is the argument and the table base left in r2 is incidental. The native table has 266 entries, bounded below by the one-byte index (256 values must all be in range) and above by the primary table base at 0x080554C0; a prior 283-entry claim reaches 0x08055504, inside the primary table, and is refuted. No native routine is reconstructed and no native index is named.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter primary slot 1 (operand reader)
targets.role: reads a variable-length sign-magnitude operand from the cursor and pushes it onto the context's value stack
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 1, entry 0x08003C8A, 52 bytes and 26 instructions. A LEAF: no calls and NO literal pool, so it needed no helper and no pool stubbing. Its only entry is primary table word 0x08003C8B, and no direct BL site targets it. The encoding read off the instructions: big-endian base-128 groups, bit 7 of each byte continues the sequence, bit 0 of the accumulator is the sign and the rest is the magnitude, extracted with an arithmetic shift. 1 byte reaches -63, 2 -8191, 3 -1048575, 4 -134217727. There is NO length limit and no validation: the only exit is a byte with bit 7 clear. The arithmetic shift makes the sign invert once accumulator bit 31 is set, so the maximal five-group sequence 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0xFF 0x7F decodes to +1 rather than -2147483647; that is recorded as the code's actual behaviour and reproduced exactly, not corrected. The value is pushed at context+0x00 (a counter) and context+4+4*index, which proves the field the interpreter zeroes at 0x0800405C is a stack counter. 'sm7' is NOT a ROM string: it is a project nickname recorded as a candidate alias only.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter value-stack consumer (primary slot 7)
targets.role: the first consumer of the value stack: pops the top value, adds it to the new top in place, and leaves the sum in the lower slot
targets.notes: primary dispatch slot 7, entry 0x08003D3E, 20 bytes and 10 instructions. The smallest function in the image holding the value-stack pop idiom, and a leaf with no calls and no literal pool. 84 functions in the VM surface contain the idiom (111 pops total; 69 native, 15 primary), so this is one of a family, but only this one is lifted. It consumes two values and produces one, a net counter delta of -1, and the result is written to the LOWER operand slot values[count-2] while the upper slot is abandoned rather than cleared. The counter is written back BEFORE the operand reads, which the underflow proves. There is NO underflow check: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, the slot address becomes context-4, and the handler decrements the word immediately BELOW the context object while touching no value slot; successive underflows walk the base four bytes further down each time. That is recorded as actual behaviour and reproduced exactly, including the 32-bit address wrap the modelling depends on. The operand order values[count-2] <op> values[count-1] is not observable in this handler because addition is commutative; it is established by the sibling at primary slot 8 (0x08003D52), which shares the first eight instructions and performs `subs r1, r2, r1`. Slots 8 and 9 are NOT lifted. No opcode table is reconstructed and no opcode index is named.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter value-stack arithmetic (primary slots 8 and 9)
targets.role: the rest of the value-stack arithmetic family: slot 8 subtracts the top from the deeper value, slot 9 multiplies them
targets.notes: primary dispatch slots 8 (0x08003D52) and 9 (0x08003D66), 20 bytes and 10 instructions each, mutually adjacent and adjacent to slot 7 which is lifted separately so its report stays reproducible. Both are leaves: no calls and no literal pool. The three tile 0x08003D3E..0x08003D7A and differ in exactly one instruction - `adds r1, r2, r1`, `subs r1, r2, r1`, `muls r2, r1, r2`. Slot 8 is the member that proves the operand order for the whole family, because addition and multiplication are commutative: `subs r1, r2, r1` computes r2 - r1, r2 holds the lower slot and r1 the top, so the shared contract is `deeper = FIRST source, top = SECOND source`. Note slot 9's combining instruction writes r2 rather than r1, so its store is `str r2,[r0]` where the others store r1; the result register differs but the slot written and the contract do not. All three are plain 32-bit operations with no saturation and no overflow branch, so `muls` keeps only the low half of a 64-bit product. There is NO underflow check in any member: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF and the arithmetic runs against the word immediately below the context object - slot 8 INCREMENTS it (deeper - 0xFFFFFFFF = deeper + 1) and slot 9 replaces it with its own negation (0xFFFFFFFF * deeper = -deeper) - while no value slot is touched, and successive underflows walk four bytes further down. Reproduced exactly, with no guard added. No opcode table is reconstructed and no opcode index is given a name beyond the operation its own instruction performs.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter surviving-value consumer (native entry 29)
targets.role: pop one value and pass it to a call, with a global field as the other argument
targets.notes: native dispatch entry 29, code address 0x080007E6, 24 bytes and 11 instructions, one terminator at 0x080007FC. A mechanical scan of both proven dispatch tables found 52 functions that pop a stack value and do NOT write a result back into the slot; this is the smallest of them, with one pop, one call, one literal and no branches. It is the first routine in the target chain that turns a surviving stack value into an actual use: it decrements the counter, reads values[count-1], and passes that value as the SECOND argument (r1) to sub_08004380, with the FIRST argument (r0) being the +0x14 field of the object at the routine's only literal 0x08054FBC. Nothing is written back to the stack, so the consumed slot keeps its old value and no result replaces it, which is what distinguishes it from the arithmetic family. Ordering is proven by the self-check reading the counter from inside the callee: the counter store precedes the value read, which precedes the call. UNDERFLOW IS HARMLESS TO MEMORY here, unlike the arithmetic family: a zero counter becomes 0xFFFFFFFF, the base becomes context-4, and [slot+4] is therefore context itself, so the value passed on underflow is the brand-new counter 0xFFFFFFFF; because the routine has no store to the slot, nothing below the context is read or written. A second underflow walks the base down and reads pre[3] instead. No guard was added. The callee is declared, not reconstructed, and no meaning is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter VM value effect (sub_08004380)
targets.role: set one bit of a byte array inside an object, from the value the VM popped
targets.notes: sub_08004380, 22 bytes and 11 instructions, one terminator at 0x08004394, no branches, NO calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF, so the effect is established by this routine alone and no helper had to be followed. Its argument contract is already proven from its caller: native dispatch entry 29 passes r0 = *(0x08054FBC + 0x14) and r1 = values[count-1] popped from the VM stack. THE CONCRETE EFFECT: it sets bit (value & 7) of the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55, preserving the other seven bits. The two shifts are the standard bit-array split - `asrs r2, r1, #3` selects the byte, `lsls r3, r1, #0x1d` then `lsrs r3, r3, #0x1d` isolates the low three bits to select the bit within it - and `orrs` plus `strb` make it a read-modify-write. THE BYTE-INDEX SHIFT IS ARITHMETIC, which matters: a value with bit 31 set gives a negative byte index and the write lands BEFORE the base. 0xFFFFFFFF maps to base + 0x54 bit 7, one byte before its unsigned position, and 0x80000000 maps to base + 0xF0000055, nowhere near the logical-shift answer of base + 0x10000055. THE RECONSTRUCTION MODELS THE ARITHMETIC SHIFT EXPLICITLY because C's right shift of a negative signed value is implementation-defined. THERE IS NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check: no compare against a size and no conditional branch exists anywhere in the routine, so every value selects a byte and that byte is written, however far outside the object it lies. No guard was added. UNKNOWN: what the bit MEANS, how large the byte array is, and what reads the bit afterwards. No name is assigned to the object, the array or the bit, and nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter bit-array reader (sub_08004364)
targets.role: test one bit of the byte array the effect routine writes, and return 0 or 1
targets.notes: sub_08004364, 28 bytes and 14 instructions, two terminators at 0x0800437A and 0x0800437E, no calls and NO literal pool. A LEAF sitting immediately before the setter sub_08004380, with the clearer sub_08004396 immediately after it, so the three tile 0x08004364..0x080043AC as one bit-array accessor trio. THE INDEX SPLIT IS IDENTICAL TO THE SETTER'S: `asrs r2, r1, #3` selects the byte and the `lsls r2, r1, #0x1d` / `lsrs r2, r2, #0x1d` pair isolates the low three bits, so it reads the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55, the same byte the setter writes. The byte-index shift is ARITHMETIC, so a value with bit 31 set reads BEFORE the base, exactly as the setter writes. IT TESTS THE BIT FOR SET: `ands` masks the byte with 1 << (value & 7) and the routine branches on whether the result is zero. THE RETURN VALUE IS A NORMALISED BOOLEAN, 0 or 1, not the masked byte, so a caller cannot see which bit was masked. IT WRITES NOTHING: there is no store anywhere in the routine, which is what makes it a reader rather than the setter or the clearer. There is NO BOUNDS CHECK and no NULL check. THE FIRST OBSERVABLE CONSEQUENCE: three call sites consume the boolean, and all three treat the bit as a predicate - at 0x080007C4 the boolean is materialised into a word slot by `str r0, [r4]`; at 0x080007DA the INVERTED boolean is materialised by `movs r1,#1 ; subs r0, r1, r0 ; str r0, [r4]`; and at 0x080032EE the boolean gates setting a bit in a packed local word (`cmp r0,#0 ; beq ; movs r0,#1 ; lsls r0,r4 ; orrs r6,r0`), a gather loop copying set bits out of the array. So the bit's first concrete consequence is that it becomes a 0/1 value in an engine slot, and one caller deliberately inverts it. WHAT THE BIT MEANS IS STILL UNKNOWN: no semantic name is assigned to the flag, the array or the object, the array's size is unknown, and what reads the materialised word afterwards is not followed. Nothing is imported from another title.

targets.name: ByteCodeInterpreter boolean materialisation (sub_080007B6, sub_080007CC)
targets.role: replace the stack top with the flag bit, and with its inverse
targets.notes: sub_080007B6 (22 bytes, 10 instructions) and sub_080007CC (26 bytes, 12 instructions), adjacent, one terminator each at 0x080007CA and 0x080007E4, one call each to the already-lifted reader sub_08004364, and one shared literal at 0x080008D8. THE DESTINATION IS THE SAME AT BOTH SITES, and it is derived rather than assumed: each computes its address as `context + count*4` from the counter at context+0x00 (`ldr r1,[r0] ; lsls r1,r1,#2 ; adds r4,r1,r0`), and the value stack holds values[i] at context + 4 + 4*i, so context + count*4 is context + 4 + 4*(count-1), which is values[count-1], THE TOP OF THE STACK. Both routines therefore REPLACE THE STACK TOP IN PLACE. This is NOT a pop: neither stores to context+0x00, so the COUNTER IS UNCHANGED, and it is not a separate word either. The two differ only in what they store: the first stores the flag (0 or 1), the second stores 1 - flag, so for a boolean input the second is the exact inverse of the first. Both return the value they stored in r0, and neither reads r1. THE STACK IS NOT CHECKED FOR BEING EMPTY: with a counter of zero the computed address is context + 0, so the word read is the COUNTER itself and the store REPLACES THE COUNTER with the flag, leaving the count at 0 or 1. No guard was added. THE FIRST CONCRETE CONSEQUENCE, proven through the already-lifted consumer sub_080007E6 which begins immediately after these two at 0x080007E6: it pops values[count-1] and passes it to sub_08004380, which sets bit (value & 7) of the byte at base + (value >> 3) + 0x55. With a materialised boolean the index is 0 or 1, so THE BOOLEAN SELECTS WHICH BIT IS SET in the first byte of the flag array - bit 0 when the tested flag was clear, bit 1 when it was set. The boolean is therefore used as a BIT INDEX by the first consumer downstream of it, not as a truth value. UNKNOWN: what either bit means, whether callers rely on the counter being untouched, and what reads the array afterwards. No semantic name is assigned, and nothing is imported from another title.
